the-past-2013.gazette: Asghar Farhadi made The Past in the suburbs of Paris, his first feature shot outside Iran, and carried his working method across the border intact: long rehearsals, a plot built from what people withhold rather than what they announce. As in About Elly, the film keeps ordinary time and lets a single withheld fact reorganize everyone in the room. The explanation that would settle it never arrives.

the-wind-rises-2013.gazette: Jiro Horikoshi was a real engineer, and Miyazaki keeps him inside the documented record — the Great Kantō earthquake of 1923, the drafting tables at Mitsubishi, the A6M Zero that came off them. The film treats the war not as a backdrop for a love story but as the thing the beautiful machine was for. Miyazaki announced his retirement the year it opened.

american-sniper-2014.gazette: Chris Kyle's memoir gave the film its spine and the Navy's documented record supplied the rest: four deployments to Iraq, the sniper's log, the returns home that went worse each time. Parts of what Kyle wrote did not survive later scrutiny, and the enemy marksman Mustafa, barely a paragraph in the book, arrives on screen as a war-long duel. The argument over the gap opened alongside the film and never really closed.
american-sniper-2014.prism: The film needed an opponent worth the whole war, so it promoted a paragraph into a nemesis. That's a storytelling repair with a political bill attached — the more legible the enemy, the less the war has to explain itself.

blind-massage-2014.gazette: Blind Massage takes place in a Nanjing massage parlour, and Lou Ye filled the cast with blind and partially sighted performers working alongside professional actors. The camera answers in kind: it slides out of focus, loses its subject, hands over to sound. Berlin gave the film its cinematography prize in 2014.

citizenfour-2014.gazette: Laura Poitras walked into a Hong Kong hotel room in June 2013 with the camera already running, which makes the footage the first record of the source rather than a reconstruction of him. Journalists worked the documents on the bed while the name Snowden reached the outside world. Citizenfour is evidence and film at once; the Academy gave it the documentary Oscar in February 2015.

still-the-water-2014.gazette: On Amami Ōshima, Naomi Kawase let the island's practices happen in front of the lens: a goat killed and butchered in one unbroken passage, animist ritual performed rather than staged. Documentary and fiction share the frame by design, and the film never marks the seam between them. It competed at Cannes in 2014.
still-the-water-2014.prism: Filming an actual slaughter buys authenticity with an animal's life, and the transaction runs one way — the goat is not a party to the realism contract. Kawase's answer is to hold the shot through all of it, which at least refuses the usual move of taking the credit and cutting away.

the-imitation-game-2014.gazette: Bletchley Park is among the best-documented secret operations of the twentieth century, declassified in pieces from 1974 onward. The Imitation Game draws on that record and rearranges it: the Bombe becomes one man's machine, colleagues become obstacles, a spy subplot arrives on cue. Turing's 1952 conviction and the pardon that came sixty-one years later are not inventions; a good deal of what surrounds them on screen is.

amy-2015.gazette: Every frame of Amy existed before Asif Kapadia began — camcorder tapes from friends, studio sessions, paparazzi video shot by the people selling her. The interviews run as voices over that footage, with no one placed on camera to explain. Winehouse's family disowned the finished film, and it won the documentary Oscar in 2016.

arabian-nights-2015.gazette: Miguel Gomes sent reporters across Portugal during the austerity years to gather what was actually happening — shipyards emptying, wages cut, families evicted — and fed those accounts into a structure borrowed from Scheherazade. The three volumes run past six hours, and the last one spends much of its length with real chaffinch trappers in the Lisbon suburbs. The testimony is not decoration; it is the material the fables are made of.
arabian-nights-2015.prism: Wrapping a foreclosure in a fairy tale is a gamble both ways: the fable can carry the grief further than a news item, or it can let a viewer file the whole thing under invention. Gomes takes the risk deliberately, and the trappers in the final volume are the receipt.

cartel-land-2015.gazette: Matthew Heineman filmed on both sides of the border — Tim Foley's armed patrols in the Arizona desert, and Dr. José Mireles's Autodefensas taking Michoacán towns back from the Knights Templar cartel. The camera stayed through the firefights and through the slower turn, when the vigilantes began to resemble what they had risen against. Mireles was arrested and imprisoned before the film was finished; the footage had already recorded the arc.

dheepan-2015.gazette: Jacques Audiard cast Antonythasan Jesuthasan, a former Tamil Tiger fighter turned novelist living in France, as a man carrying a dead stranger's papers into a Paris housing estate. Most of the film is observed at the level of paperwork: asylum interviews, language classes, a caretaker's ring of keys. Then the last reel hands everything to a genre the previous two hours had refused, and the film took the Palme d'Or anyway.

mountains-may-depart-2015.gazette: Jia Zhangke set the first section in his own hometown of Fenyang in 1999, then widened the frame with each jump forward — 1999, 2014, and a 2025 that had not yet happened when he shot it. Coal money, emigration, a boy named Dollar: the film tracks what the boom did to a family's capacity to speak to one another. Jia has been filming the same transformation, largely in the same province, since the 1990s.
mountains-may-depart-2015.prism: The widening aspect ratio is the joke and the diagnosis in one gesture — more picture, less contact. By the final section a son needs a translator to talk to his own mother, which is a fair accounting of what thirty years of growth cost that household.

mustang-2015.gazette: Mustang was shot in a village on Turkey's Black Sea coast and submitted to the Academy by France, where its director had spent most of her life. The film presents its account of rural patriarchy — the house sealed with bars, the virginity checks, the marriages arranged in sequence — as observed fact. Turkish critics contested precisely that, arguing the customs on screen belonged to an outsider's idea of the countryside rather than the countryside itself.

our-little-sister-2015.gazette: A year passes in Kamakura and the plot is mostly chores: plums picked from the garden tree and put up as wine, whitebait on toast, a funeral, the walk to the station. Kore-eda declines to dramatize any of it upward. The household's buried history surfaces instead in what gets cooked and who is willing to eat it.

son-of-saul-2015.gazette: Members of the Sonderkommando buried written accounts in the ground around the Birkenau crematoria, and some of those pages were dug up after the war as the Scrolls of Auschwitz. László Nemes worked from that testimony and from the October 1944 revolt, then built the film to match its vantage: a narrow lens locked to one man's face, the killing kept at the blurred edge of the frame and carried by sound. It took the Grand Prix at Cannes in 2015 and the foreign-language Oscar the following year.
son-of-saul-2015.prism: Keeping the atrocity out of focus is not delicacy; it is a rule about who is permitted to look. The Sonderkommando saw all of it and were meant to die carrying it, so the film grants exactly their allowance of vision and nothing beyond it.
